plan.title: How Costco Really Makes Money (It's Not the Groceries)
plan.description:
Costco sells around $270 billion of goods a year, but its profit story is really about the membership card. We use Costco's fiscal 2025 annual report to show how fees, thin margins and 90%+ renewal rates fit together.

Chapters:
0:00 The surprising number
0:51 Fees vs profit
1:33 Thin margins on purpose
2:27 Renewal rates
3:02 Gold Star vs Executive
4:02 Fewer products, more power
4:55 The full model

segments.narration: Costco sold almost two hundred and seventy billion dollars of stuff last year. And yet, the groceries, the TVs and the giant packs of toilet paper are not really how it makes its money.
To see where the money actually comes from, we need to look at one small plastic card. Let's open up Costco's own annual report and follow the numbers.

In its 2025 fiscal year, which ended on the last day of August, Costco reported net sales of about two hundred and seventy billion dollars. That is the money customers paid at the checkout for products.
On top of that, it collected about five point three billion dollars in membership fees. That is the yearly fee people pay just for the right to walk through the door.
Now here is the number that changes how you see the whole business. Costco's net income for the year, the profit left after paying for everything, was about eight point one billion dollars.
Put those side by side. Membership fees of five point three billion. Total profit of eight point one billion. The fees alone are equal to roughly two thirds of the company's entire profit.

And unlike product sales, a membership fee has almost no cost attached to it. Costco does not have to buy a pallet of anything to earn it. Most of that money drops straight through to the bottom line.
So how does the store side of the business look? Costco's gross margin in 2025 was about eleven point one percent.

In plain words, for every hundred dollars of goods Costco sells, only about eleven dollars is left after paying for the goods themselves. And that eleven dollars still has to cover wages, rent, electricity and trucks.
Most supermarkets keep a much bigger slice of each sale. Costco deliberately keeps its slice thin, so its prices stay low, so members feel the fee is worth paying.
That is the trick. The store is designed to roughly break even on products, and the membership is designed to make the profit.
Low prices keep members happy. Happy members renew. Renewals pay the fees. And the fees fund the low prices. It is a loop that feeds itself.
How strong is that loop? According to Costco, about ninety two percent of members in the United States and Canada renewed in 2025. Worldwide the figure was close to ninety percent.
For a subscription business, that is a remarkable number. Many streaming services and gym chains would be thrilled to keep nine out of ten customers every single year.
And there are a lot of members. At the end of fiscal 2025, Costco had about eighty one million paid memberships, across nine hundred and fourteen warehouses around the world.
There are two main tiers. The basic Gold Star membership in the United States costs sixty five dollars a year.
The Executive membership adds another sixty five dollars on top, for one hundred and thirty dollars in total, and gives members a cash reward on what they spend.
That upgrade matters more than it looks. About thirty eight point seven million members were on the Executive tier, close to half of all paid members.
Executive members pay double the fee, and they tend to shop more often and spend more, because they are earning a reward on every purchase.
Costco also raised its fees in the United States and Canada on the first of September 2024. Even after that increase, renewal rates stayed above ninety percent.
When a company can raise its price and almost nobody leaves, that tells you customers see real value in what they are paying for.
The other part of the machine is simplicity. Costco says a typical warehouse carries fewer than four thousand active products at any one time.
A regular supermarket might carry tens of thousands. Fewer products means Costco can buy each one in enormous volume, and that buying power is what lets it squeeze suppliers for low prices.

Fewer products also means less shelf work, less storage and faster stock turnover. The warehouses themselves are plain concrete buildings with goods stacked on pallets, which keeps running costs down.
Then there is Kirkland Signature, Costco's own brand. The company describes it as a growing portion of its sales.
Own brand products let Costco control quality and price, and they give members one more reason they can only get this deal by renewing their card.
So if we put it all together, the model looks like this.

Step one, charge a yearly fee. Step two, use that guaranteed income to keep prices so low that the store barely profits on the goods. Step three, keep the range small, buy in huge volume, and run lean warehouses.
Step four, members feel they save more than the fee, so more than nine in ten come back. And the cycle starts again.
That is why Costco can sell close to two hundred and seventy billion dollars of goods on thin margins and still earn about eight billion dollars in profit.
The real product Costco sells is not the hot dog or the rotisserie chicken. It is the membership card, and everything inside the warehouse exists to make that card feel worth renewing.
